blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Poisson regression models a count outcome that follows a Poisson distribution (recall §5.7.1.3) with a log link: log(expected count) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + … (+ offset). exp(b) is an IRR when a person-time offset is present (recall §13.4).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Counts cannot be negative; the log link keeps predicted counts positive, as the logit kept probabilities inside 0 to 1 (recall §13.1). The Poisson distribution has one parameter: its variance equals its mean. That single fact makes Poisson regression simple, and it is also its weak point (§13.6).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The malaria data of §13.4: log(expected cases) = log(population) + b₀ + b₁ × near_water. The number of antenatal visits a woman makes, modelled on distance and wealth, is another Poisson-type outcome (here without an offset, since every woman has one pregnancy).

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
ml <- read.csv("data/malaria_villages.csv")
p1 <- glm(cases ~ near_water + offset(log(population)),
          family = poisson, data = ml)
summary(p1)$coefficients
exp(cbind(IRR = coef(p1), confint.default(p1)))
# no offset
p0 <- glm(cases ~ near_water, family = poisson, data = ml)
exp(coef(p0))

                    IRR       2.5 %     97.5 %

near_water  2.300178412 1.828495725 2.89353738
(Intercept)  near_water 
  23.600000    1.618644

With the offset, exp(intercept) = 0.00874 is the rate away from water (8.74 per 1,000), and exp(b₁) = 2.30 (1.83 to 2.89) is the IRR. The SE of b₁, 0.117, is exactly √(1/191 + 1/118) from §13.4: with one binary predictor, Poisson regression reproduces the hand calculation. Without the offset, the intercept is the mean count per village (23.6) and exp(b₁) = 1.62 is the count ratio.

points.html: Poisson regression assumes that events occur independently and that the variance equals the mean. Check both.

Does the model apply here? Malaria is vector-borne. Cases in one village share mosquitoes, breeding sites and each other’s parasites, so they are not independent events. Expect the counts to vary more than Poisson allows; §13.6 checks this.
When the assumption fails, the IRR estimate may still be reasonable, but its SE and CI are too small.
